title: Norton's Theorem: Any Linear Circuit Becomes One Current Source
topic: Norton's theorem — any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a short-circuit current I_N in parallel with the same R_N = R_th; source transformation swaps freely between Thévenin and Norton

beats.narration: Thévenin gave us a voltage source. What if we want a current source instead?

elements.content: Same network — viewed as a current source.

beats.narration: Short the terminals together. The current that flows through that wire is I Norton — the short-circuit current of the network.

elements.content: Two-source three-resistor network with terminals a and b shorted by a wire
Ammeter symbol in the shorting wire reading I_N
Charge dots flowing through the shorting wire

beats.narration: A Thévenin form on the left morphs into a Norton form on the right. The resistance is the same; the source flips from V Thevenin over R Thevenin volts to V Thevenin over R Thevenin amps in parallel.

elements.content: Side-by-side: V_th + R_th in series feeding R_L on the left morphs into I_N + R_N in parallel feeding R_L on the right; both share the same I_L through the load.
Transformation arrow between the two with R_N = R_th and I_N = V_th / R_th labels

beats.narration: Reconnect a load. The current source splits between R Norton and the load by the current-divider rule — and you get exactly the same I L as Thevenin predicted.

elements.content: Norton equivalent driving a load R_L: I_N current source on the left, R_N in parallel, R_L to the right; charge dots split between R_N and R_L
Current arrows on each branch — I_L into R_L, the rest into R_N

beats.narration: Pick whichever form makes the algebra easier — same load current either way.

elements.content: Thévenin and Norton are two faces of the same network.
(in series → in parallel, just divide V_th by R_th)
